title: What was running on this computer? A first look at a RAM dump
short: First look at a RAM dump
lead: Memory holds what a disk does not: running programs, open network connections and code that never touched a file. This workflow is a first pass over a Windows memory dump with Volatility 3. It shows what each plugin prints and how to read it.
time: 2 to 3 hours on a practice dump
evidence: A memory (RAM) dump of a Windows computer
answers: Which programs were running when memory was captured
What command line each program was started with
Which processes deserve a closer look
need: A memory dump file, or a practice dump (see the practice section on this page)
Volatility 3 installed. It needs Python 3.8 or newer. The vol command is added when you install it with pip
An internet connection on first use, so that Volatility can download the Windows symbol files it needs from Microsoft. Offline symbol packs also exist
Free disk space of at least the size of the dump, for hashes, notes and exported data

steps.title: Capture memory first, if the computer is still on
steps.text: Memory is lost when the computer is switched off, so capture it before anything else. Run the capture tool from a USB drive and save the dump to a different drive, not to the computer's own disk. For example, WinPmem is started with the output file name as its argument. Note the time, the tool and its version, then hash the dump straight away.
steps.note: Running a capture tool changes a small part of memory. That is accepted practice, but write down that you did it. Use the exact file name of the tool version you have; it differs between releases.

steps.title: Hash the dump and check that Volatility can read it
steps.text: Calculate the dump's hash value and write it down. Then run the info plugin. It prints rows such as Kernel Base, Is64Bit, NtMajorVersion, NtMinorVersion and SystemTime. If you see them, the dump is readable. SystemTime is the moment the dump was taken, so every time you read later is compared with it. The first run can take several minutes while symbols download.
steps.note: If vol is not found, run python3 vol.py from the Volatility 3 folder instead. In Volatility 3 every Windows plugin starts with windows. and there is no --profile option.

steps.title: List the processes as a tree
steps.text: pstree lists the processes Windows was tracking and indents each child under its parent. The columns include PID, PPID, ImageFileName, Threads, CreateTime, ExitTime, and recent versions add Audit, Cmd and Path. Compare with normal Windows: services.exe and lsass.exe are started by wininit.exe, svchost.exe by services.exe, and there is one copy of lsass.exe. Flag odd names, odd parents (a document program starting a command shell) and odd paths.

steps.title: Look for hidden or finished processes
steps.text: pslist walks the list that Windows keeps. psscan ignores that list and searches memory for process records, so it can find processes that ended (they show an ExitTime) or that were unlinked from the list. Put the PID columns of both outputs side by side. A PID that only psscan shows needs an explanation: ended normally, or hidden. Neither answer is proof by itself.

steps.title: Read the command lines
steps.text: cmdline prints PID, Process and Args: the full text the program was started with, including options and file names. This often explains what a flagged process was doing, for example which archive an archive program had open. If a process is listed with no arguments, part of its memory may have been paged out. Check pstree for the same process.

steps.title: List network connections
steps.text: netscan prints Offset, Proto, LocalAddr, LocalPort, ForeignAddr, ForeignPort, State, PID, Owner and Created. State shows LISTENING, ESTABLISHED or CLOSED for TCP. Match the PID to the processes you flagged. The plugin's source lists support up to Windows 10 build 20348 on 64-bit systems. For newer builds try windows.netstat, which walks the network tables instead of scanning, and read both outputs with care.

steps.title: Flag possible injected code
steps.text: malfind lists memory regions of a process that are executable and also writable, or that changed after loading. Columns include PID, Process, Start VPN, End VPN, Protection (for example PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE), a hexdump and a disassembly. A Notes entry that mentions an MZ header means the region starts like a program file. Many normal programs trigger it, so use it only on processes you already doubted. Add --pid to focus on one.

steps.title: Browse the dump a second way
steps.text: MemProcFS presents the same dump as a drive of folders and files. On Windows it needs the Dokany file system driver, and it mounts as drive M: by default. Open the folder of a process you flagged and compare its name, PID and parent with what Volatility printed. Adding the option -forensic 1 starts its forensic mode, which can also write CSV files.

steps.title: Cross-check and write it down
steps.text: Keep each plugin's output as a text file. Record the Volatility version, the exact commands, the dump's hash value, the Windows version from windows.info and the SystemTime. Mark every item as a lead or as confirmed by a second source, and say which source it was.

artifacts.name: windows.info
artifacts.tells: Windows version, 32 or 64 bit, and SystemTime, the time of the dump

artifacts.name: windows.pslist and pstree
artifacts.tells: Processes Windows was tracking, with PID, parent PID, start time and exit time

artifacts.name: windows.psscan
artifacts.tells: Process records found by scanning, including ended or unlinked ones

artifacts.name: windows.cmdline
artifacts.tells: The command line each process was started with

artifacts.name: windows.netscan
artifacts.tells: Connections and listening ports, with the owning process and a created time

artifacts.name: windows.malfind
artifacts.tells: Memory regions that may hold injected code (leads only)

artifacts.name: MemProcFS drive
artifacts.where: Mounted view of the dump (M: by default)
artifacts.tells: The same processes as folders, for a second look

limits: A memory dump shows one moment. It does not show what happened before, except for traces that happened to remain.
Memory changes while it is being captured, so some records can be inconsistent or damaged.
malfind and similar plugins produce false alarms. A flagged process is not proof of malware.
If the computer was switched off before capture, live memory is gone. A hibernation file or page file on the disk may hold part of it.
Volatility needs symbol files that match the Windows build. Without them, plugins fail. Network plugins may not support the newest builds.
Plugin names, columns and options change between Volatility versions. Check the documentation for the version you install.

practice.name: MemLabs
practice.text: A set of free practice labs for memory forensics in a capture-the-flag style: Lab 0 to Lab 6, from easy to hard. All dumps are from Windows computers. Each lab has its own folder in the repository. Lab 1, called Beginner's Luck, is rated easy. A published write-up of Lab 1 describes a Windows 7 SP1 64-bit dump that is hosted on a file-sharing site. The main page gives no download link, so look in the lab folder. Only Lab 0 has a detailed walkthrough. The others are checked by e-mailing flags to the authors, so there is no public answer key.
practice.task: Open the Lab 1 folder, download the dump and hash it. Run steps 2 to 7 of this workflow. Write down the Windows version, the time of the dump, the processes that look out of place with their parents, and the command line of each. Find the process whose command line names a file, and say what that suggests.
practice.note: The page for the repository does not list file sizes or a published hash, so record your own hash. If a download link no longer works, use another lab or make your own dump from a test computer.

learn.label: Volatility 3 documentation: getting started on Windows
Volatility 3 on GitHub (install, symbols, first commands)
Volatility 3 source: windows.malfind (shows exactly how regions are chosen)

mistakes: Saving the memory dump to the computer's own disk. This overwrites data you may still need. Save to a separate drive.
Using Volatility 2 commands such as --profile or a bare pslist. In Volatility 3 the plugin is windows.pslist and the profile is found from symbols.
Reading only pslist. A hidden or finished process does not appear there, so always compare with psscan.
Treating a malfind hit as proof of malware. Many normal programs create executable regions.
Forgetting the dump time. Process start times only mean something when read against SystemTime from windows.info.
verify: Compare the process list from pstree with the process folders in MemProcFS for the same dump. Names and PIDs should agree.
Check the Windows version and build from windows.info against the disk image or the case notes of the same computer.
For a remote address from netscan, look for the same address in firewall logs or a packet capture from the same time.
Run the same plugin a second time and compare the outputs. Hash the dump before and after you work to show it did not change.
report_line: A memory dump taken on [date and time, time zone] with [tool and version] (SHA-256 [value]) was examined with Volatility 3 [version]. windows.info reported [Windows version]. Process [name], PID [number], parent [name], was started with the command line [text]. This is a lead and was not yet confirmed by a second source.
